The Q&A clusters on exactly the right worries. The most important subtle signal is structural, not verbal: this company spent 2023–2024 in a wrenching takeover fight. Classify the trajectory as turning (PIVOTING): the business is mid-pivot from a lost Microsoft-incentive model and a failed sale process into a larger, merger-built, cash-generative reseller with a credible margin-expansion plan. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is the reported-versus-adjusted earnings gap: you are underwriting cash flow and a self-help synergy plan, not a clean, growing GAAP earnings stream — so the thesis lives or dies on whether the CHF 80–100M of synergies and the >23% adjusted-margin target actually flow through to reported profit over the next several quarters, and on a North America turn that is promised but unproven.

On the economic moat: SoftwareOne is a reseller and services intermediary. Its edge is real but narrow — switching costs and procurement complexity (clients lean on it to navigate Microsoft, AWS, Google, Adobe and now multi-vendor and sovereign-cloud rules), plus newly enlarged scale. But the returns evidence is mixed: return on invested capital is about 10.7% (decent) while net margins are near zero and gross margin is contracting (44.1%, flagged contracting). That is a narrow moat, roughly stable, not a wide one. The genuine secular question is AI: large language models and agentic tools could compress the value of "good-enough" advisory and software-procurement work over time. Management actually leans into this as opportunity (guiding customers on which AI models to deploy), and a procurement/licensing intermediary is less directly displaceable than a knowledge-work shop — so the structural threat is manageable, not terminal, but it is the right thing to watch.

# SoftwareOne Holding AG (SWON.SW) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Listing: SIX Swiss Exchange, all figures in Swiss francs (CHF) unless noted. Live price at review: CHF 8.495 (2026-07-11), market value about CHF 1.82 billion, roughly 215 million shares outstanding.*

SoftwareOne is a global reseller and advisor for software and cloud services — it helps 70,000-plus companies buy, license, optimize and run software from vendors like Microsoft, AWS, Google and Adobe, and it manages their software estates (what the industry calls software asset management, or SAM). In July 2025 it completed a transformational merger with Crayon, a Norwegian rival, roughly doubling its scale. The stock is being screened as a "deep value" idea: it trades on about seven to eight times free cash flow (the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment) with a clean, net-cash balance sheet, yet its reported accounting profit is near zero.

---

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The single transcript we hold is the full-year 2025 results call (2026-03-31), so we read the arc through that call plus the multi-year financial trajectory rather than a sequence of quarters. The story management is telling has clearly shifted from "defend the base" to "we have built a new, larger company and now we compound it."

Three threads dominate. First, **the Crayon combination is the whole story now** — "2025 was transformational... we have created a global software and cloud leader," opening with combined gross sales of CHF 14 billion, 13,000 employees, 70-plus countries. Everything else is framed against that new, larger canvas. Second, **a return to growth after a stall**: management leans on like-for-like revenue up 1.4% for the full year "ahead of our initial expectation of broadly flat," accelerating to "11% revenue growth" in the fourth quarter. Third, **self-help economics** — cost synergies (savings from combining the two firms) running at CHF 64 million by the call, since raised to CHF 86 million against an CHF 80-100 million target, and an adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, stripped of one-off costs) held "above 20%."

What was quietly dropped is the old takeover drama. Nothing in this call references the 2023-2024 saga in which US private-equity firm Bain Capital, backed by the founding shareholders, chased the company at around CHF 18.80 per share and was rebuffed. That chapter is closed: the founders instead pushed through the Crayon deal as the alternative path, and management now speaks purely as operators of a standalone growth plan — a posture cemented at the Capital Markets Day on 2026-06-09, which set 2030 targets with no mention of a sale.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (FY2025 call) | The hard numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "2025 was transformational... returned to growth, revenue up 1.4% like-for-like, Q4 +11%" | Screener revenue +22.5% year-on-year to CHF 1.24 billion (that jump is mostly the six months of Crayon consolidated, not organic); reported (IFRS) EBITDA CHF 181.5 million on CHF 1.24 billion revenue = about 14.6% | Broadly supported, but the headline growth is acquisition-driven; the honest organic number is the +1.4% like-for-like, which is modest |
| "Profitability remained strong, adjusted EBITDA margin 20.9%" | Reported operating profit CHF 57.8 million; net income just CHF 0.9 million; the gap between the ~20.9% adjusted margin and the ~14.6% reported margin is the "adjustments" (integration and restructuring costs) | Real but flattering — the adjusted figure is a fair proxy for underlying earnings power, yet accounting profit is essentially nil, so you are trusting the add-backs |
| "Good progress on synergies... CHF 64 million run-rate" (now CHF 86 million) | Consistent with the improving margin trajectory; free cash flow (trailing twelve months) about CHF 228 million, an 11% free-cash-flow yield | Supported — this is the most credible part of the story; cash generation is genuine |
| "We do not see any headwinds from the EA incentive changes" in 2026 (Microsoft enterprise-agreement rebates) | North America revenue fell 12.6% in 2025 partly on these changes; the company beat 0 of the last 7 quarterly earnings expectations | Partly supported — Q4 rebounded, but the vendor-incentive dependence is a proven source of negative surprises |
| Net-cash strength | Balance sheet confirms cash and short-term investments of CHF 434 million against total debt (leases) of CHF 74.5 million — net cash of roughly CHF 345-360 million, about CHF 1.6 per share | Verified — a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back |

The core tension: the story is **richer than the GAAP profit-and-loss but roughly matched by the cash flow**. Earnings per share collapsed from CHF 0.76 (2021) to CHF 0.006 (2025) — a five-year decline of about 70% a year — which looks alarming until you see it is driven by integration costs, purchase-accounting amortization from Crayon, and a larger share count, not by cash going backwards. Free cash flow, by contrast, is healthy and growing.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, from a low base.** The FY2025 call is confident and forward-leaning. Co-CEO Melissa Mulholland: "The actions we are taking are working... a stronger position to drive momentum in 2026." CFO Hanspeter Schraner on North America — the biggest sore spot (revenue −12.6%) — is unusually specific and offensive rather than defensive: "I'm very confident that in North America 2026, we will return into growth... I also expect in Q1 a better performance than in Q4." Management repeatedly turns risks into opportunities: Microsoft price rises "help our business," and the rise of AI vendors like Anthropic and OpenAI is "additional partner opportunity... our business model really thrives around complexity."

The language has shifted from the defensive, cost-focused register of the 2022-2024 turnaround years toward growth and investment ("we are continuing to invest in our technology, especially in the platforms"). That is a genuine tonal upgrade — but it rests on only two quarters of combined-company results, so confidence outruns the track record.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Medium.** The positive: management set expectations of "broadly flat" revenue for 2025 and delivered +1.4% like-for-like — a small, clean beat — and it is running ahead on synergies (CHF 86 million versus an CHF 80-100 million target). The Q4 acceleration to +11% was real. The negative, and it is material: the screener shows the company **beat 0 of its last 7 quarterly consensus prints (0%)**, earnings per share have fallen every way you cut them, and the whole board was replaced in 2024 amid a shareholder revolt. This is not a management team with a long, unblemished delivery record; it is a reconstituted board and a newly-merged operating team two quarters into a two-year integration. Reliability score: **Medium**, trending up if the 2026 margin guidance (adjusted EBITDA above 23%) is hit.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Analysts pressed hardest on three seams. **(1) Microsoft incentive changes** (Kepler Cheuvreux's Florian Treisch): whether the enterprise-agreement rebate cuts stay a headwind — management insists 2026 will see "stabilization," but this is the exact line item that has burned the model before. **(2) Impairment risk** (Berenberg's Andreas Wolf): whether more write-downs are coming after the CHF 8 million Latin America impairment — Schraner's answer ("no further impairments expected... otherwise you would have impaired already") is a hostage to fortune if any region's plan slips. **(3) Exceptional/adjustment costs** (UBS's Christopher Tong): the recurring question of how big the "one-off" adjustments really are — management's promise to hold them "below CHF 30 million" excluding Crayon costs is the tell that the gap between reported and adjusted profit is the number the market distrusts most. The unaddressed worry underneath all three: how durable is a reseller's margin when its biggest supplier (Microsoft) keeps changing the rules and AI is starting to automate the advisory work.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Reported profit is essentially zero** (net income CHF 0.9 million in 2025) and earnings quality screens weak (Piotroski 3 of 9). You are underwriting adjusted numbers, not GAAP.
🔴 **Vendor concentration and incentive risk** — Microsoft rebate changes drove a 12.6% North America decline; the model's margin is partly at a supplier's discretion.
🔴 **Contracting gross margin** (44.1%, flagged declining; about 0.74 standard deviations below its historical peak) as mix shifts toward lower-margin resale — a slow squeeze on the value the company captures.
🔴 **Thin post-merger track record** — only two quarters of combined results; integration and cross-sell are promised, not proven.
🟢 **Genuine, growing free cash flow** — about CHF 228 million trailing, an 11% yield, on a capital-light model.
🟢 **Clean, net-cash balance sheet** — roughly CHF 345-360 million net cash, no debt wall, funding the dividend and buybacks from a position of strength.
🟢 **Synergies ahead of plan** (CHF 86 million of an CHF 80-100 million target) and a credible 2030 margin path (adjusted EBITDA toward 28% from ~21%).
🟢 **AI framed as demand, not just threat** — the reseller thrives on vendor complexity, and more AI vendors means more advisory need in the near term.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important quiet signal is **the change in segment reporting** (Raphael Erb: "our operating segments have been reassessed... Nordics, Western Europe and CEE"). Re-cutting the regions right after a large merger makes year-on-year comparison harder and gives management more latitude in how the combined numbers are presented — worth watching, not yet damning. Second, the **impairment answer** is a subtle forward-looking commitment: by saying no further write-downs are expected, management has staked credibility on every region's plan holding. Third, the **AI framing is doing double duty** — management genuinely sees near-term upside from complexity, but the same breath ("we help guide our customers around which model makes sense") describes exactly the advisory task that generative AI is most likely to automate over a longer horizon. Finally, the **absence of any takeover language** is itself a signal: the founders, who own roughly 29% and once tried to sell the company, are for now backing a standalone plan — the buyout optionality is dormant, not dead.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING — but early, and cheap for quality-adjusted reasons, not because the market has missed a hidden crown jewel.** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the special-situation catalyst that made this name interesting — the Bain/Apax/CVC take-private — is spent.** It resolved into the Crayon merger (completed 2025-07-02), Bain walked, and the June 2026 Capital Markets Day laid out a purely standalone plan. What remains is a real but ordinary operational turnaround: cheap on cash flow, net cash, a credible margin runway, but with the stock already re-rated about 46% off its CHF 5.83 low to near its 52-week high, and no hard, dated event left to force the remaining gap closed.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat is switching costs and scale in software asset management and multi-vendor cloud advisory — sticky relationships with 70,000 clients and privileged status with hyperscalers (it became Google Cloud's first global authorized distributor in early 2026). But it is a channel/advisory position, not hard lock-in, and the value it captures is partly set by its suppliers. **Moat trend: STABLE** — adjusted margins are expanding on synergies even as gross margin mix-shifts down, so the durable earnings base is holding, not visibly eroding. **Secular threat: MATERIAL (not terminal).** Two forces bear on terminal value — generative AI automating the licensing-optimization and advisory work that is part of the company's value-add, and hyperscalers periodically re-cutting partner economics (the Microsoft incentive saga). Near-term these read as tailwinds (more vendors, more complexity, more advisory demand); long-term they cap pricing power. This is a fear-tempered value case, not a value trap — but it is not a wide-moat compounder either, so size it as a moderate-conviction, wait-for-a-better-entry idea rather than an aggressive one.

# SoftwareOne Holding AG (SWON.SW) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared for the investment committee. Listing: SIX Swiss Exchange, all figures in Swiss francs (CHF) unless noted. Live price at review: CHF 8.495 (2026-07-11), market value about CHF 1.82 billion, roughly 215 million shares outstanding.*

SoftwareOne is a global reseller and advisor for software and cloud services — it helps 70,000-plus companies buy, license, optimize and run software from vendors like Microsoft, AWS, Google and Adobe, and it manages their software estates (what the industry calls software asset management, or SAM). In July 2025 it completed a transformational merger with Crayon, a Norwegian rival, roughly doubling its scale. The single transcript we hold is the full-year 2025 results call (2026-03-31), so we read the arc through that call plus the multi-year financial trajectory rather than a sequence of quarters. The story management is telling has clearly shifted from "defend the base" to "we have built a new, larger company and now we compound it."

Three threads dominate. First, **the Crayon combination is the whole story now** — "2025 was transformational... we have created a global software and cloud leader," opening with combined gross sales of CHF 14 billion, 13,000 employees, 70-plus countries. Everything else is framed against that new, larger canvas. Second, **a return to growth after a stall**: management leans on like-for-like revenue up 1.4% for the full year "ahead of our initial expectation of broadly flat," accelerating to "11% revenue growth" in the fourth quarter. Third, **self-help economics** — cost synergies (savings from combining the two firms) running at CHF 64 million by the call, since raised to CHF 86 million against an CHF 80-100 million target, and an adjusted profit margin (adjusted EBITDA — earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, stripped of one-off costs) held "above 20%."

What was quietly dropped is the old takeover drama. CHF 64 million run-rate" (now CHF 86 million) | Consistent with the improving margin trajectory; free cash flow (trailing twelve months) about CHF 228 million, an 11% free-cash-flow yield | Supported — this is the most credible part of the story; cash generation is genuine |

The most important quiet signal is **the change in segment reporting** (Raphael Erb: "our operating segments have been reassessed... Nordics, Western Europe and CEE"). Third, the **AI framing is doing double duty** — management genuinely sees near-term upside from complexity, but the same breath ("we help guide our customers around which model makes sense") describes exactly the advisory task that generative AI is most likely to automate over a longer horizon. Finally, the **absence of any takeover language** is itself a signal: the founders, who own roughly 29% and once tried to sell the company, are for now backing a standalone plan — the buyout optionality is dormant, not dead.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING — but early, and cheap for quality-adjusted reasons, not because the market has missed a hidden crown jewel.** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **the special-situation catalyst that made this name interesting — the Bain/Apax/CVC take-private — is spent.** It resolved into the Crayon merger (completed 2025-07-02), Bain walked, and the June 2026 Capital Markets Day laid out a purely standalone plan. This is a single-quarter read, not a multi-quarter arc, so the trajectory work below leans more on the financial trajectory the screener supplies than on a sequence of calls. A note on identity: the peer-group file in our system tags SWON.SW as "Swisscom AG" — that is wrong. SWON.SW is SoftwareOne Holding AG, a Swiss-listed software and cloud reseller and services firm that, in mid-2025, merged with its Norwegian rival Crayon. Every number and quote below is SoftwareOne's.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The single call we have is dominated by one story: 2025 was "transformational" because SoftwareOne combined with Crayon to create what management calls "a global software and cloud leader," with roughly CHF 14 billion of combined gross sales, more than 70,000 clients across 70-plus countries, and about 13,000 employees. The reported income statement blends twelve months of SoftwareOne with six months of Crayon (the deal consolidated from July 1, 2025), which is why headline revenue jumped about 22.5% year over year to CHF 1.24 billion even though the underlying, like-for-like growth of the combined business was a modest 1.4%.

The arc within the year is a recovery story. Management is at pains to show that growth troughed early — hurt by Microsoft cutting the incentives it pays resellers on enterprise agreements — and then accelerated through the year, "back to positive territory" by the third quarter and reaching 11% revenue growth in the fourth. The drivers they lean into now are the transition from those lost enterprise-agreement incentives toward cloud subscription (CSP) and services-based incentives, a fast-growing channel (distribution) business led by Asia-Pacific, and a newly announced role as the first global authorized distributor for Google Cloud. AI is introduced as an emerging tailwind rather than a delivered number — they talk about partnering with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI and about Microsoft price increases helping their cost-optimization pitch.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (FY2025 call) | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "We returned to growth… up 1.4% like-for-like, accelerating to 11% in Q4" | Reported revenue +22.5% (mostly the Crayon consolidation); underlying combined growth only 1.4% for the year | Honest — they clearly separate reported from like-for-like, and the 1.4% is genuinely soft |
| "Profitability remained strong… adjusted EBITDA margin 20.9%" | Net margin 0.1%; reported EBITDA margin 16.7%. The gap between a ~21% adjusted figure and a near-zero net margin is enormous | The "adjusted" number hides heavy real costs — integration, acquisition, amortization. Reported net income was about CHF 0.9 million on CHF 1.24 billion of sales |
| "Good progress on synergies — CHF 43M run-rate by end-2025, CHF 64M today, target CHF 80–100M" | Free cash flow is genuinely strong: trailing-twelve-month FCF about CHF 228M, P/FCF ~5.2x, FCF margin 16.3% | Mixed-to-credible. The central forensic tension is the chasm between a ~21% *adjusted* profitability story and a *reported* net margin of essentially zero. ## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

With only one call, this is a snapshot, not a trend. The tone is confident and forward-leaning: "2025 was transformational," "the actions we are taking are working," and on the worst region, North America (-12.6% in 2025), the CFO says he is "very confident" growth returns in 2026 and expects Q1 to beat Q4. Management is specific where it helps them (synergy run-rates, the Google Cloud distribution win, segment growth rates) and notably reassuring on the Microsoft incentive headwind that scared the market in 2024 — they now say they "do not see any headwind effect" from enterprise-agreement changes in 2026. We cannot track a multi-call guide-versus-deliver record from one transcript, so credibility has to be inferred. Two things cut against management: a hard beat record of 0 of 7 quarters (per the screener) and a long history of erratic net income. Two things cut for them: the 1.4% like-for-like growth "ahead of our initial expectation of broadly flat," and adjustment costs that came in below the promised CHF 30M ceiling. The cleanest credibility signal is external and current: subsequent reporting shows the company *raised* its 2026 outlook (to mid-to-high single-digit constant-currency revenue growth and an adjusted EBITDA margin target above 23%, up from ~20.9%), with synergies tracking to the top of the range. On balance, reliability is Medium — the cash and synergy delivery is real, but the long record of weak reported earnings keeps this short of High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The Q&A clusters on exactly the right worries. Analysts pressed on (a) whether the Microsoft enterprise-agreement headwind is truly behind them — management says yes, even a possible tailwind in 2026; (b) further impairments after the CHF 8M LATAM write-down — the CFO says none are expected because they test at the regional level annually and would have taken them already; (c) exceptional/adjustment costs in 2026 — they reiterate the below-CHF-30M ceiling but explicitly carve out Crayon integration costs, which is the soft spot, since those carve-outs are where the reported-versus-adjusted gap lives; and (d) the timing of the North America turnaround, which is promised but not yet shown.

🔴 North America fell 12.6% in 2025 on self-inflicted sales-execution problems; the recovery is a promise.

🟢 Genuinely strong, cheap cash flow: trailing FCF about CHF 228M at roughly 5.2x, a 16.3% FCF margin, and FCF up sharply year over year.
🟢 A real net-cash balance sheet (about CHF 360M) — rare for a company this optically distressed.
🟢 Concrete, partly-delivered self-help: CHF 64M of synergies in hand against an CHF 80–100M target, and a margin guide raised to above 23%.
🟢 A credible strategic logic — scale in software/cloud distribution, the Google Cloud authorized-distributor win, and a real AI-advisory angle.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important subtle signal is structural, not verbal: this company spent 2023–2024 in a wrenching takeover fight. Private-equity firm Bain Capital made repeated bids (down to about CHF 18.8 per share); the board rejected them; the founding shareholders, who control roughly 29%, ousted that board to reopen the door — and then, in March 2024, dissolved their group with Bain and walked away. The Crayon merger is what management did *instead* of selling. So the takeover catalyst that once animated this name is spent, and the company is now a self-help integration story, not a deal story. The second signal is linguistic: the relentless framing of profitability as "adjusted" and the explicit carve-out of Crayon costs from the adjustment ceiling — management is steering attention to cash and run-rates and away from a still-thin reported bottom line.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Classify the trajectory as turning (PIVOTING): the business is mid-pivot from a lost Microsoft-incentive model and a failed sale process into a larger, merger-built, cash-generative reseller with a credible margin-expansion plan. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is the reported-versus-adjusted earnings gap: you are underwriting cash flow and a self-help synergy plan, not a clean, growing GAAP earnings stream — so the thesis lives or dies on whether the CHF 80–100M of synergies and the >23% adjusted-margin target actually flow through to reported profit over the next several quarters, and on a North America turn that is promised but unproven.

On the economic moat: SoftwareOne is a reseller and services intermediary. Its edge is real but narrow — switching costs and procurement complexity (clients lean on it to navigate Microsoft, AWS, Google, Adobe and now multi-vendor and sovereign-cloud rules), plus newly enlarged scale. But the returns evidence is mixed: return on invested capital is about 10.7% (decent) while net margins are near zero and gross margin is contracting (44.1%, flagged contracting). That is a narrow moat, roughly stable, not a wide one. The genuine secular question is AI: large language models and agentic tools could compress the value of "good-enough" advisory and software-procurement work over time. Management actually leans into this as opportunity (guiding customers on which AI models to deploy), and a procurement/licensing intermediary is less directly displaceable than a knowledge-work shop — so the structural threat is manageable, not terminal, but it is the right thing to watch.

# Forensic Dossier — SoftwareOne Holding AG (SWON.SW)

*One earnings call available: full-year 2025 results, reported 2026-03-31. This is a single-quarter read, not a multi-quarter arc, so the trajectory work below leans more on the financial trajectory the screener supplies than on a sequence of calls. A note on identity: the peer-group file in our system tags SWON.SW as "Swisscom AG" — that is wrong. SWON.SW is SoftwareOne Holding AG, a Swiss-listed software and cloud reseller and services firm that, in mid-2025, merged with its Norwegian rival Crayon. Every number and quote below is SoftwareOne's.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The single call we have is dominated by one story: 2025 was "transformational" because SoftwareOne combined with Crayon to create what management calls "a global software and cloud leader," with roughly CHF 14 billion of combined gross sales, more than 70,000 clients across 70-plus countries, and about 13,000 employees. The reported income statement blends twelve months of SoftwareOne with six months of Crayon (the deal consolidated from July 1, 2025), which is why headline revenue jumped about 22.5% year over year to CHF 1.24 billion even though the underlying, like-for-like growth of the combined business was a modest 1.4%.

The arc within the year is a recovery story. Management is at pains to show that growth troughed early — hurt by Microsoft cutting the incentives it pays resellers on enterprise agreements — and then accelerated through the year, "back to positive territory" by the third quarter and reaching 11% revenue growth in the fourth. The drivers they lean into now are the transition from those lost enterprise-agreement incentives toward cloud subscription (CSP) and services-based incentives, a fast-growing channel (distribution) business led by Asia-Pacific, and a newly announced role as the first global authorized distributor for Google Cloud. AI is introduced as an emerging tailwind rather than a delivered number — they talk about partnering with the likes of Anthropic and OpenAI and about Microsoft price increases helping their cost-optimization pitch.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim (FY2025 call) | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "We returned to growth… up 1.4% like-for-like, accelerating to 11% in Q4" | Reported revenue +22.5% (mostly the Crayon consolidation); underlying combined growth only 1.4% for the year | Honest — they clearly separate reported from like-for-like, and the 1.4% is genuinely soft |
| "Profitability remained strong… adjusted EBITDA margin 20.9%" | Net margin 0.1%; reported EBITDA margin 16.7%. The gap between a ~21% adjusted figure and a near-zero net margin is enormous | The "adjusted" number hides heavy real costs — integration, acquisition, amortization. Reported net income was about CHF 0.9 million on CHF 1.24 billion of sales |
| "Good progress on synergies — CHF 43M run-rate by end-2025, CHF 64M today, target CHF 80–100M" | Free cash flow is genuinely strong: trailing-twelve-month FCF about CHF 228M, P/FCF ~5.2x, FCF margin 16.3% | Mixed-to-credible. The cash generation is real and cheap; the synergy figures are self-reported run-rates, not yet in net income |
| Balance sheet strength implied | Recomputed net cash of about CHF 360M (cash ~CHF 434M vs ~CHF 74M debt) | Confirmed — a real, sizable cushion and a true add to intrinsic value |
| Multi-year earnings power | Five-year EPS CAGR -70%; net income swung 2021 CHF 118M → 2022 -CHF 58M → 2024 -CHF 2M → 2025 +CHF 0.9M; earnings beat 0 of 7 quarters | The bottom line has been erratic and weak for years; only cash flow has held up |

The central forensic tension is the chasm between a ~21% *adjusted* profitability story and a *reported* net margin of essentially zero. The cash flow statement rescues the picture — this business converts revenue to cash well — but the income statement has not produced reliable earnings in years (a five-year EPS decline of about 70% a year, zero earnings beats in the last seven quarters).

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

With only one call, this is a snapshot, not a trend. The tone is confident and forward-leaning: "2025 was transformational," "the actions we are taking are working," and on the worst region, North America (-12.6% in 2025), the CFO says he is "very confident" growth returns in 2026 and expects Q1 to beat Q4. Management is specific where it helps them (synergy run-rates, the Google Cloud distribution win, segment growth rates) and notably reassuring on the Microsoft incentive headwind that scared the market in 2024 — they now say they "do not see any headwind effect" from enterprise-agreement changes in 2026. The posture is offensive (growth, AI, channel expansion) rather than defensive, though the heavy reliance on the word "adjusted" is itself a quiet defensive tell.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

We cannot track a multi-call guide-versus-deliver record from one transcript, so credibility has to be inferred. Two things cut against management: a hard beat record of 0 of 7 quarters (per the screener) and a long history of erratic net income. Two things cut for them: the 1.4% like-for-like growth "ahead of our initial expectation of broadly flat," and adjustment costs that came in below the promised CHF 30M ceiling. The cleanest credibility signal is external and current: subsequent reporting shows the company *raised* its 2026 outlook (to mid-to-high single-digit constant-currency revenue growth and an adjusted EBITDA margin target above 23%, up from ~20.9%), with synergies tracking to the top of the range. On balance, reliability is Medium — the cash and synergy delivery is real, but the long record of weak reported earnings keeps this short of High.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

The Q&A clusters on exactly the right worries. Analysts pressed on (a) whether the Microsoft enterprise-agreement headwind is truly behind them — management says yes, even a possible tailwind in 2026; (b) further impairments after the CHF 8M LATAM write-down — the CFO says none are expected because they test at the regional level annually and would have taken them already; (c) exceptional/adjustment costs in 2026 — they reiterate the below-CHF-30M ceiling but explicitly carve out Crayon integration costs, which is the soft spot, since those carve-outs are where the reported-versus-adjusted gap lives; and (d) the timing of the North America turnaround, which is promised but not yet shown.

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 Reported net margin of essentially zero (0.1%) against a ~21% adjusted figure — the adjustments are large and recurring-looking (integration, acquisition, amortization), so "adjusted" profitability flatters a business that has barely earned a net profit in five years.
🔴 A weak solvency score (Altman-Z around 0.6) and a low quality score (Piotroski 3 of 9) — though the Altman reading is distorted by the merger accounting and the genuine net-cash position.
🔴 North America fell 12.6% in 2025 on self-inflicted sales-execution problems; the recovery is a promise.
🔴 A history of zero earnings beats in seven quarters and a 70%-a-year five-year EPS decline.
🟢 Genuinely strong, cheap cash flow: trailing FCF about CHF 228M at roughly 5.2x, a 16.3% FCF margin, and FCF up sharply year over year.
🟢 A real net-cash balance sheet (about CHF 360M) — rare for a company this optically distressed.
🟢 Concrete, partly-delivered self-help: CHF 64M of synergies in hand against an CHF 80–100M target, and a margin guide raised to above 23%.
🟢 A credible strategic logic — scale in software/cloud distribution, the Google Cloud authorized-distributor win, and a real AI-advisory angle.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most important subtle signal is structural, not verbal: this company spent 2023–2024 in a wrenching takeover fight. Private-equity firm Bain Capital made repeated bids (down to about CHF 18.8 per share); the board rejected them; the founding shareholders, who control roughly 29%, ousted that board to reopen the door — and then, in March 2024, dissolved their group with Bain and walked away. The Crayon merger is what management did *instead* of selling. So the takeover catalyst that once animated this name is spent, and the company is now a self-help integration story, not a deal story. The second signal is linguistic: the relentless framing of profitability as "adjusted" and the explicit carve-out of Crayon costs from the adjustment ceiling — management is steering attention to cash and run-rates and away from a still-thin reported bottom line.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

Classify the trajectory as turning (PIVOTING): the business is mid-pivot from a lost Microsoft-incentive model and a failed sale process into a larger, merger-built, cash-generative reseller with a credible margin-expansion plan. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing is the reported-versus-adjusted earnings gap: you are underwriting cash flow and a self-help synergy plan, not a clean, growing GAAP earnings stream — so the thesis lives or dies on whether the CHF 80–100M of synergies and the >23% adjusted-margin target actually flow through to reported profit over the next several quarters, and on a North America turn that is promised but unproven.

On the economic moat: SoftwareOne is a reseller and services intermediary. Its edge is real but narrow — switching costs and procurement complexity (clients lean on it to navigate Microsoft, AWS, Google, Adobe and now multi-vendor and sovereign-cloud rules), plus newly enlarged scale. But the returns evidence is mixed: return on invested capital is about 10.7% (decent) while net margins are near zero and gross margin is contracting (44.1%, flagged contracting). That is a narrow moat, roughly stable, not a wide one. The genuine secular question is AI: large language models and agentic tools could compress the value of "good-enough" advisory and software-procurement work over time. Management actually leans into this as opportunity (guiding customers on which AI models to deploy), and a procurement/licensing intermediary is less directly displaceable than a knowledge-work shop — so the structural threat is manageable, not terminal, but it is the right thing to watch.
